beats.got: The promise is output that sounds like me and not like everyone else. I don't yet know what a guardrail is.

beats.got: A teaser. I'm curious but not committed yet.

beats.trigger: The first exchange became context.

beats.trigger: Tools, goals, checks, boundaries, and loops come later and depend on it.

beats.trigger: You write it once, and it shapes every answer.

beats.trigger: Change the context, watch the agent's output shift, then package what you learned for the next session.
beats.got: The plan is clear. I will make a personal site, which is a bit remote from my work.

beats.trigger: The mess is the point.
beats.got: I paste my whole LinkedIn page and get a generic site. Fine as a baseline. I do wonder about pasting personal data into a tool.

beats.trigger: A colleague who lands on it should think *"this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at,"*
beats.got: The site is meant to make colleagues want to work with me. That I like.

beats.trigger: The LLM already knows StoryBrand, so you don't reproduce the questions.
beats.got: I can name a method I know and tell it how to adapt. For HR that could be a competency model or a change model.

beats.trigger: The agent walks you through the five tuned beats.
beats.got: It interviews me one beat at a time and I answer briefly. That is easy and a bit fun.

beats.trigger: Your strengths shape how the whole site sounds.
beats.got: My strengths go in and the tone changes. Simple, and it works.

beats.trigger: Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall for five minutes on what they're great at.
beats.got: Listing what I hate is easier than listing strengths, and inverting it gives sharper identity. That is true of me.

beats.trigger: Vague input drifts back to the statistical-default you.
beats.got: Specific complaints work and vague categories don't. I could use this for role descriptions.

beats.got: It names generic claims about me, but I can't yet judge whether it was honest about them.

beats.got: I can say a brand's name and get its look. A fun trick, but nothing to do with people questions.

beats.trigger: The chat summary rounds corners; the file is what travels
beats.got: The agent writes my lessons into a rules file that a fresh session or a colleague can reuse. That is how a habit spreads from one person to a team.

beats.trigger: The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.
beats.got: Every phase added context, and each time the output got more mine.

beats.trigger: The LLM didn't get better between Phase 1 and Phase 6. You got better at feeding it the context that produces YOUR output.
beats.got: The skill is mine, not the tool's. That is a learning point I could take to my leadership team. I'd like an HR example here instead of compliance reviews and product strategy.

beats.trigger: ## Iterate and Learn
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The move: change something, notice what shifted, adjust, build again.
beats.got: A recap of the exercise: change, notice, adjust.

beats.trigger: Grading its own work is another chance to be helpful: the self-report is the same kind of output as the thing reported on.
beats.got: The agent is too nice when it checks its own work. That is a real warning for anything HR would trust it with.

beats.trigger: Where the account matches what you remember, you have two reads agreeing.
beats.got: Treat the agent's report as a claim and check it against what I saw myself.

beats.trigger: Only you could catch a wrong line about you
beats.got: My knowledge is the test. For people decisions that means the human stays the judge.

beats.trigger: Nobody knows where agents are going, not Anthropic, not your board.
beats.got: Learning by doing beats reading reports. Nobody has the answer on headcount, which is honest, but it didn't give me one.

beats.trigger: The second pass is where the file starts compounding.
beats.got: The agent reviews the rules file against what happened and rewrites it. I expect it to change a lot.

beats.trigger: **compound interest on a rule file.**
beats.got: Keep correcting the rules file and it gets better each round. A team could own one and sharpen it together.

beats.trigger: Your gut on what is uniquely you carries more weight than the agent's.
beats.got: A second, independent reader gives a cleaner opinion, and my gut still outranks it.

take_homes: What I tell the AI first changes everything it says after. A sentence about who I am, or a real list of complaints, beats a vague request.
Write the lessons into a file so a fresh session, or a colleague, starts from them. That is how a habit could spread from me to my HR partners.
The agent is too kind about its own work, so I check its report against what I know.

monday.move: Try a short rules file for one HR task, such as a first draft of a role description, and show it to one HR partner.
monday.who: Me, then one HR business partner
monday.when: Tuesday afternoon, after my leadership meeting
monday.stop_condition: If the file needs real employee data in the tool, I stop until the DPO and works council have been asked.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet.

misconception.why: We spent the module on a personal site and rules files, and nobody said anything about which roles change. The line that nobody knows where agents are going was honest, but I still don't have a headcount answer for my leadership team.

one_line: Good at showing that specific context beats generic output, but it's about a personal website and I'm still asking what it means for my people.
